title: Startup d-Matrix Will Pair Its Raptor Memory-Based XPU To Nvidia Rackscale Iron
gist: Inference-accelerator startup d-Matrix, funded with more than $500 million, is plugging its memory-centric Raptor XPU into Nvidia's MGX NVL144 rack architecture rather than building its own rack, betting that riding Nvidia's deployed ecosystem is the fastest path into datacenters; the piece frames disaggregated inference (GPUs for prefill, memory-centric XPUs for decode) as the emerging structure of AI serving.

insights.claim: Demand for low-latency inference has exploded over the past twelve months, driven by agentic AI tools such as Anthropic's Claude Code and the introduction of OpenClaw, pushing inference workloads past what Nvidia and AMD GPUs can handle on their own.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Agentic coding tools are the concrete workload driving a structural shift in silicon demand from training to latency-sensitive decode — a new TAM for non-GPU accelerators.
insights.quote: Over the last twelve months, there has been an explosion of low-latency inference across many different applications
insights.locator: Engineers with startup d-Matrix have spent

insights.claim: The arrival of cybersecurity applications is named as a new source of huge demand for low-latency tokens, indicating inference demand is broadening beyond chat and coding into security tooling.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Watch security vendors as an underappreciated incremental buyer of inference capacity.
insights.quote: Now, with the arrival of cybersecurity applications, low latency tokens are in huge demand.

insights.claim: d-Matrix was founded in 2019 to attack inference specifically, at a time when, per its CEO, 'not many people even knew what inference was' — a seven-year development cycle before shipping its first product.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Illustrates the 7-year silicon lead time that makes AI hardware bets hard to time and hard to copy quickly.
insights.locator: The company has been focused on inferencing since its founding

insights.claim: d-Matrix's XPU approach tightly couples memory such as SRAM or 3D-RAM with GPUs and CPUs in the same rack to accelerate token generation and cut cost, a memory-centric rather than compute-centric design philosophy.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: If decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, value accrues to memory/packaging suppliers rather than to raw FLOPS vendors.
insights.locator: The XPU tightly couples the memory

insights.claim: In a disaggregated inference deployment, GPUs handle the compute-intensive prefill phase where context tokens are processed, while memory-centric accelerators handle the decode phase where the model generates responses.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Prefill/decode disaggregation is the wedge that lets non-Nvidia silicon into Nvidia racks without displacing the GPU.
insights.locator: In a disaggregated environment, GPUs are best

insights.claim: d-Matrix executives claim its Corsair inference platform, launched in June after more than $500 million of funding including from Microsoft's M12 venture arm, can run inference workloads ten times faster than Nvidia GPUs alone.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A vendor-claimed 10x gap is the kind of number that, if independently verified, reprices the inference silicon landscape.
insights.locator: After seven years of development, d-Matrix

insights.claim: The Raptor platform will tape out by the end of 2026 and ship in Q4 2027, using a 4-nanometer TSMC compute die fused atop a custom DRAM die at a 36-micron pitch to deliver 100 TB/sec of bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A concrete 2027 delivery date and TSMC dependency to track against Nvidia's own Vera-Rubin cadence.
insights.locator: Raptor, which will tape out by the end of the year

insights.claim: Raptor uses a variant of the chip-on-wafer package currently used for HBM packaging, combining a DRAM memory chip with an SRAM compute chip — putting d-Matrix in direct competition for the same advanced packaging capacity as HBM.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Advanced packaging capacity, not design, is the binding constraint — another claim on the same TSMC/OSAT bottleneck.
insights.locator: With Raptor, D-Matrix uses a variant of the chip-on-wafer package

insights.claim: The Lightning platform, featuring a multi-high DRAM stack, sits behind Raptor on d-Matrix's roadmap and is also covered by the Nvidia partnership, indicating a multi-generation commitment rather than a one-off product deal.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Partnership scope across future generations reduces the single-product risk in the startup's story.
insights.locator: The partnership will also include future versions

themes.theme: Nvidia MGX as an open-but-captive platform

insights.claim: d-Matrix chose to plug Raptor into Nvidia's MGX reference architecture and AI factory offering rather than build its own liquid-cooled rack, on the reasoning that Raptor needs a 'house to put it in' and Nvidia is already deployed in every datacenter in the world.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Rack-level standardization is becoming Nvidia's real moat — challengers distribute through Nvidia rather than around it.
insights.quote: This is truly the fastest way we feel of getting this amazing path-breaking technology that we are building at D-Matrix into the market with quick scale, with a robust supply chain to back it up
insights.locator: A new partnership with Nvidia will help d-Matrix

insights.claim: d-Matrix's rack will reuse Nvidia's NVLink compute tray, NVLink switch tray, Vera CPUs, Bluefield DPUs, and ConnectX/Spectrum-X networking, substituting only Raptor XPUs for Vera-Rubin GPUs inside the liquid-cooled NVL144 rack.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Even a 'competitor' rack still buys Nvidia CPUs, DPUs, NICs and switches — Nvidia monetizes the challenger's success.
insights.locator: Key to d-Matrix's plans is NVLink and NVSwitch

insights.claim: Nvidia frames its architecture as 'completely fungible' and 'vertically integrated, but horizontally open,' with NVLink Fusion ports opening the platform to third-party silicon and vendors free to take as much or as little of the Nvidia stack as they want.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Nvidia's openness strategy converts would-be rivals into content inside its rack — bullish for Nvidia's attach rate, bearish for pure rack-level challengers.
insights.locator: Jesse Clayton, principal product marketing manager

insights.claim: A single d-Matrix NVL144 rack will hold 144 Raptor XPUs with 2.3 TB of 3D-stacked DRAM running at 100 TB/sec per card, for an aggregate memory bandwidth of 7.2 petabytes per second, and can also be run as a companion to Nvidia Vera-Rubin racks.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Companion-rack deployment means incremental spend on top of, not instead of, GPU racks — expands total AI capex rather than splitting it.
insights.locator: The rack also will feature 2.3 TB of 3D-stack DRAM

themes.theme: AI factory economics and measured performance

insights.claim: Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said the AI factory platform revenue opportunity has grown from roughly $18 billion per gigawatt with 2022 Grace-Hopper rackscale systems to $40 billion per gigawatt with forthcoming Vera-Rubin systems.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Dollar content per gigawatt has more than doubled in four years — the key multiplier turning power buildout into Nvidia revenue.
insights.locator: Nvidia's AI factory business is expanding rapidly

insights.claim: At Hot Chips 2026, a rack of d-Matrix Raptor chips delivered about 3,000 tokens per second per user on Z.ai's GLM 5.2 and about 1,000 tokens per second per user on Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, with the vendor claiming it can scale this across eight racks.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Per-user token rates on open Chinese frontier models are the new benchmark currency for inference silicon.
insights.locator: At Hot Chips, d-Matrix showed the results

insights.claim: d-Matrix's stated business premise is doing more inference per unit of money, time and energy so as to eventually 'alleviate the need to build out more datacenters' — an explicit bet against the assumption that AI demand must be met with ever more physical capacity.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A credible efficiency curve is the main bear case for the datacenter and power buildout trade; watch whether efficiency gains get absorbed by demand instead.
insights.quote: We can hopefully, over time, alleviate the need to build out more datacenters.
insights.locator: Our entire approach is predicated on doing more

insights.claim: d-Matrix built its rack-scale credibility partly through M&A, acquiring GigaIO's datacenter business in April and launching the SquadRack reference design with Arista Networks, Broadcom, and Supermicro.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Names the second-tier beneficiaries — Arista, Broadcom, Supermicro — that get pulled along by every new accelerator entrant.
insights.locator: Building off of its acquisition in April
